claim: Drosophila melanogaster possesses four α-tubulin genes
source: Drosophila melanogaster possesses four α-tubulin genes.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript text without supporting data shown in this manuscript, but is presented as established knowledge.

claim: Three α-tubulin genes (αTub84B, αTub84D, and αTub67C) are expressed during oogenesis and early embryogenesis
source: Three of them are expressed during oogenesis and early embryogenesis, suggesting that they contribute to the formation of microtubules during these stages. The three genes are αTub84B, αTub84D, and αTub67C (Kalfayan and Wensink, 1982).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kalfayan and Wensink, 1982

claim: αTub84B and αTub84D differ in only two amino acids
source: αTub84B and αTub84D differ in only two amino acids.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: The primary sequence in the C-terminal domain of αTub84B and αTub84D is identical
source: Their primary sequence in the C-terminal domain is identical, and both are expressed in most tissues and throughout development.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: αTub67C is expressed exclusively during oogenesis
source: In contrast, αTub67C is expressed exclusively during oogenesis, where it is maternally loaded into the egg and embryo. The primary structure of αTub67C is distinctively different from αTub84B/D (Theurkauf et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by citation to Theurkauf et al., 1986

claim: αTub67C has phenylalanine (F) as the last residue while αTub84B/D have tyrosine (Y)
source: These differences are also apparent in the C-terminal domain and include the last residue phenylalanine (Phe, F) in αTub67C and tyrosine (Tyr, Y) in αTub84B/D.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about the protein sequences

claim: αTub85E is mainly expressed in the testes but not in the ovaries
source: αTub85E is the fourth α-tubulin. It is mainly expressed in the testes but not in the ovaries (Kalfayan and Wensink, 1982).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kalfayan and Wensink, 1982

claim: Glutamylation adds one or more glutamic acids to the sidechains of glutamic acid residues in the C-terminal tails of both α- and β-tubulin
source: Glutamylation is a PTM that adds one or more glutamic acids (Glu, E) to the sidechains of glutamic acid residues in the C-terminal tails of both α- and β- tubulin, causing the formation of a branched peptide chain (Eddé et al., 1990; Redeker et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eddé et al., 1990 and Redeker et al., 1992

claim: Enzymes that catalyze glutamylation, glycylation, and tyrosination belong to the Tubulin-tyrosine-ligase-like (TTLL) family
source: The enzymes that catalyze glutamylation, glycylation, and tyrosination belong to the Tubulin-tyrosine-ligase-like (TTLL) family (Janke et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Janke et al., 2005

claim: The TTLL family in D. melanogaster encompasses 11 genes
source: In D. melanogaster, this family encompasses 11 genes (flybase.org).
evidence: Supported by reference to FlyBase database

claim: Artificial tethering of 10E peptides to the sidechains at position E445 of α-tubulin and E435 of β-tubulin increased the processivity of kinesin motors by 1.5-fold for kinesin-1
source: Artificial tethering of 10E peptides to the sidechains at position E445 of α-tubulin and E435 of β-tubulin by maleimide chemistry increased the processivity (the run length) of kinesin motors on tubulin. For kinesin-1, this was a 1.5-fold increase (Sirajuddin et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sirajuddin et al., 2014

claim: Dynein/dynactin motors preferred a Tyr at the C-term of α-tubulin to initiate processive transport in vitro
source: In contrast to kinesin, Dynein/dynactin motors preferred a Tyr at the C-term of α-tubulin to initiate processive transport in vitro because the motor favored this isotype as an attachment point to dock onto the MTs (McKenney et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to McKenney et al., 2016

claim: Loss of both TTLL3 and TTLL8 perturbed sperm motility, causing male subfertility in mice
source: In vitro fertility assays showed that the lack of both TTLL3 and TTLL8 perturbed sperm motility, causing male subfertility in mice. Structural analyses further suggested that loss of glycylation perturbed the coordination of axonemal dynein, thus affecting the flagellar beat (Gadadhar et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gadadhar et al., 2021

claim: CG31108 is the homolog of the mammalian TTLL5 gene and was named DmTTLL5 or TTLL5
source: CG31108 is considered to be the homolog of the mammalian TTLL5 gene and was therefore named DmTTLL5 or TTLL5 (Devambez et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Devambez et al., 2017

claim: TTLL5 is required for α-tubulin glutamylation in the Drosophila nervous system
source: It is required for α-tubulin glutamylation in the Drosophila nervous system (Devambez et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Devambez et al., 2017

claim: The N-terminal core domain of TTLL5 provides the catalytic activity and is highly conserved in Drosophila TTLL5
source: The N-terminal core domain was shown to provide the catalytic activity of TTLL5 and is highly conserved in Drosophila TTLL5 (van Dijk et al., 2007, Natarajan et al., 2017; Table 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to van Dijk et al., 2007 and Natarajan et al., 2017, and reference to Table 1

claim: Drosophila TTLL5 mRNA is expressed at high levels in ovaries according to FlyBase data
source: According to FlyBase data, Drosophila TTLL5 mRNA is expressed at high levels in ovaries (Supplementary file 1), even higher than in the nervous system where initial studies were performed (Devambez et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by reference to FlyBase data in Supplementary file 1 and citation to Devambez et al., 2017

claim: The absence of TTLL1-mediated polyglutamylation of α-tubulin increased the overall motility of mitochondrial transport in axons in mice
source: An in vivo mouse study showed that the absence of TTLL1-mediated polyglutamylation of α-tubulin increased the overall (both anterograde and retrograde) motility of mitochondrial transport in axons (Bodakuntla et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bodakuntla et al., 2021

claim: Vesicular axonal transport was not affected by the absence of TTLL5-mediated α-tubulin glutamylation in the segmental nerves of Drosophila larvae
source: However, another study in Drosophila showed that the vesicular axonal transport was not affected by the absence of TTLL5-mediated α-tubulin glutamylation in the segmental nerves of larvae (Devambez et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Devambez et al., 2017

claim: In wild-type ovaries, αTub84B+D mRNAs are 4.7× as highly expressed as αTub67C according to FlyBase
source: According to FlyBase, αTub84B+D mRNAs are 4.7× as highly expressed as αTub67C.
evidence: Supported by reference to FlyBase database

claim: Mass spectrometry analysis identified a similar ratio (4.6×) of total C-terminal peptides between αTub84B/D and αTub67C
source: We identified a similar ratio (4.6×) of total C-terminal peptides by the MS analysis (Table 2A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by MS data presented in Table 2A and Supplementary file 1

claim: The general Drosophila α-tubulins αTub84B/D, but not the ovarian-specific αTub67C, showed glutamylation on their C-terminal tails in wild-type ovarian extracts
source: Analyses of wild-type ovarian extracts revealed that the general Drosophila α-tubulins αTub84B/D, but not the ovarian-specific αTub67C, showed glutamylation on their C-terminal tails (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by MS data in Supplementary file 1

claim: For αTub84B/D, sidechain glutamylation was identified on all four glutamyl residues in the C-terminal tail region: Glu443, Glu445, Glu448, and Glu449
source: For αTub84B/D, sidechain glutamylation was identified on all four glutamyl residues in the C-terminal tail region, Glu443, Glu445, Glu448, and Glu449 (Figure 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by MS data shown in Figure 1 and Supplementary file 1

claim: The most extended sidechains identified were 3Es in wild-type ovaries
source: The most extended sidechains identified were 3Es in wild-type ovaries (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1

claim: In wild-type ovaries, 71% of C-terminal peptides of αTub84B/D were modified with glutamylation (50% with 1E, 14% with 2Es, and 7% with 3Es)
source: Wild-type ovaries revealed that 71% of the peptides were modified, 50% with 1E, 14% with 2Es, and 7% with 3Es (Table 2B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative MS data presented in Table 2B

claim: In TTLL5pBac/- mutants, 4% (1 out of 24) mono-glutamylation was observed
source: On the other hand, 4% (1 out of 24) mono-glutamylation was observed in TTLL5pBac/- and no glutamylation in TTLL5MiEx/- mutants (Table 2B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by MS data in Table 2B and Supplementary file 1

claim: No glutamylation was observed in TTLL5MiEx/- mutants
source: On the other hand, 4% (1 out of 24) mono-glutamylation was observed in TTLL5pBac/- and no glutamylation in TTLL5MiEx/- mutants (Table 2B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by MS data in Table 2B and Supplementary file 1

claim: Drosophila TTLL5 is needed for the sidechain glutamylation of the C-terminal Glu443, Glu445, Glu448, and Glu449 of αTub84B/D
source: This clearly shows that Drosophila TTLL5 is needed for the sidechain glutamylation of the C-terminal Glu443, Glu445, Glu448, and Glu449 of αTub84B/D, and it appears to affect already the addition of the first Glu.
evidence: Inference based on MS data showing loss of glutamylation in TTLL5 mutants

claim: The GT335 antibody reacts with the first glutamate on the glutamate sidechain even if it is polyglutamylated
source: This antibody reacts with the first glutamate on the glutamate sidechain even if it is polyglutamylated (Figure 3A; Wolff et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wolff et al., 1992 and shown in Figure 3A

claim: In TTLL5 mutants, the GT335 signal is strongly reduced or absent but reappears in rescued ovary extracts
source: In the mutants, the signal in the corresponding region is strongly reduced or absent but reappears in the rescued ovary extracts (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B

claim: TTLL5 is required for monoglutamylation of α-tubulin
source: This result, therefore, supports the finding that TTLL5 is required for monoglutamylation of α-tubulin, and it shows that the antibody signal is specific and can be used to monitor Drosophila TTLL5 activity.
evidence: Inference based on western blot data with GT335 antibody

claim: The GT335 signal primarily arises from the glutamylation on the consecutive Glu residues E448 and E449 in the sequence -GAEEY in Drosophila α-tubulin
source: Consequently, the GT335 signal primarily arises from the glutamylation on the consecutive Glu residues E448 and E449 in the sequence -GAEEY.
evidence: Inference based on known antibody specificity and Drosophila α-tubulin sequence

claim: The 1D5 antibody recognizes α-tubulin with an -XEE sequence at the C-terminal α-carboxylate group
source: The 1D5 antibody recognizes α-tubulin with an -XEE sequence at the C-terminal α-carboxylate group (with X being a variable residue) (Rüdiger et al., 1999; Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rüdiger et al., 1999 and shown in Figure 3C

claim: Control ovaries displayed high cross-reactivity of 1D5 with a polypeptide of the predicted size, indicating the presence of glutamate sidechains containing at least two glutamates
source: In our results, the control ovaries displayed high cross-reactivity of 1D5 with a polypeptide of the predicted size. This observation indicates the presence of glutamate sidechains containing at least two glutamates, as well as the possibility of C-terminally de-tyrosinated α-tubulin (Gadadhar et al., 2017; Preston et al., 1979; Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 3D and citations

claim: TTLL5 mutants showed a strongly reduced 1D5 signal, indicating that loss of TTLL5 function prevents normal polyglutamylation
source: Consistent with the MS analysis, the TTLL5 mutants showed a strongly reduced signal with 1D5, indicating that loss of TTLL5 function prevents normal polyglutamylation.
evidence: Supported by western blot data with 1D5 antibody

claim: Overexpression of TTLL5 in TTLL5pBac/- and TTLL5Mi/- resulted in a stronger 1D5 signal and an upshifted band, suggesting hyperglutamylation on α-tubulin
source: Overexpression of TTLL5 in TTLL5pBac/- and TTLL5Mi/- even resulted in a stronger 1D5 signal and an upshifted band, suggesting the occurrence of hyperglutamylation on α-tubulin (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3D

claim: The endogenous levels of TTLL5 are typically limited in ovaries under normal conditions
source: These findings not only demonstrate the important role of TTLL5 in facilitating the glutamylation of α-tubulin but also suggest that the endogenous levels of TTLL5 are typically limited in ovaries under normal conditions.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that overexpression leads to hyperglutamylation

claim: Most of the murine TTLL5 residues involved in α-tubulin glutamylation are conserved in Drosophila TTLL5
source: Most of the murine TTLL5 residues involved in α-tubulin glutamylation are conserved in Drosophila TTLL5 (Table 1; Natarajan et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment in Table 1 and citation to Natarajan et al., 2017

claim: Drosophila TTLL5 residues K282 and E517 correspond to mouse K131 and E336, respectively, and directly interact with ADP/ATP
source: Drosophila TTLL5 residues K282 and E517 correspond to mouse K131 and E336, respectively. They directly interact with ADP/ATP and thus affect general TTLL5 enzymatic activity (Natarajan et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Natarajan et al., 2017

claim: TTLL5R339 corresponds to mouse TTLL5R188, which is vital for TTLL5's glutamylation activity
source: TTLL5R339 corresponds to mouse TTLL5R188, which is vital for TTLL5's glutamylation activity. MmTTLL5R188 resides in the β6–7 loop, which forms a salt-bridge interaction with the C-terminal tail of α-tubulin and orients it toward the ATP/ADP-binding site (van Dijk et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to van Dijk et al., 2007

claim: The glutamylation of α-tubulin was impaired in all TTLL5 mutants where the conserved residue (K282, E517, R339) was replaced
source: Western blotting results showed that the glutamylation of α-tubulin was impaired in all these TTLL5 mutants where the conserved residue was replaced (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3F

claim: The mutations of conserved residues did not abolish the stability of the corresponding mutant TTLL5 protein
source: Since these mutations did not abolish the stability of the corresponding mutant protein (Appendix 1—figure 1), our results revealed the importance of E517, K282, and R399 of Drosophila TTLL5 for glutamylation.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Appendix 1—figure 1

claim: Replacement of Drosophila TTLL5P522 prevented glutamylation of α-tubulin in Drosophila ovaries
source: Even though the importance of TTLL5P371 for glutamylation has not been reported in mammalian systems, its replacement prevented glutamylation of α-tubulin in Drosophila ovaries.
evidence: Supported by western blot data showing loss of glutamylation in P522 mutant

claim: P522 is a novel critical residue not only for the tubulin tyrosination by TTL but also for the glutamylation function of TTLL5
source: This identifies P522 as a novel critical residue not only for the tubulin tyrosination by TTL but also for the glutamylation function of TTLL5.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data showing loss of glutamylation in P522 mutant

claim: Western blotting revealed minimal or no alterations in the levels of tyrosinated α-tubulin in any of the null or CRISPR/Cas9 generated point mutants of TTLL5
source: Western blotting revealed minimal or no alterations in the levels of tyrosinated α-tubulin in any of the null or CRISPR/Cas9 generated point mutants of TTLL5.
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B, F and G

claim: The overexpression of TTLL5 did not affect the levels of tyrosinated α-tubulin
source: Additionally, the overexpression of TTLL5 did not affect these levels either (Figure 3B, F and G).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B, F and G

claim: The levels of TTLL5 do not appear to affect the levels of tyrosinated α-tubulin in ovaries
source: Thus, the levels of TTLL5 do not appear to affect the levels of tyrosinated α-tubulin in ovaries.
evidence: Inference based on western blot data

claim: The anti-mono Gly antibody TAP952 did not reveal a clear signal at the predicted position in wild-type ovaries
source: However, even in the wild-type control, the anti-mono Gly antibody TAP952 did not reveal a clear signal at the predicted position (Appendix 1—figure 2), suggesting that α-tubulin is not glycylated in Drosophila ovaries.
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Appendix 1—figure 2

claim: α-tubulin is not glycylated in Drosophila ovaries
source: However, even in the wild-type control, the anti-mono Gly antibody TAP952 did not reveal a clear signal at the predicted position (Appendix 1—figure 2), suggesting that α-tubulin is not glycylated in Drosophila ovaries.
evidence: Inference based on lack of antibody signal in Appendix 1—figure 2

claim: The known Drosophila polyglycylases (TTLL3A/B) are not expressed in ovaries
source: Furthermore, considering that the known Drosophila polyglycylases (TTLL3A/B) were shown to be the main glycylases in the whole fly and are not expressed in ovaries (Rogowski et al., 2009; Supplementary file 1), the current evidence does not justify further analysis of glycylation in Drosophila ovaries.
evidence: Supported by citation to Rogowski et al., 2009 and expression data in Supplementary file 1

claim: Specific 1D5 immunofluorescence signals were observed in the follicle cells and oocytes throughout the previtellogenic, middle, and late oogenesis stages
source: Specific 1D5 immunofluorescence signals were observed in the follicle cells and oocytes throughout the previtellogenic, middle, and late oogenesis stages (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4

claim: In stage 10B (S10B) oocytes, the 1D5 signal showed a slightly biased localization in the cortical region of the oocyte
source: In stage 10B (S10B) oocytes, the 1D5 signal showed a slightly biased localization in the cortical region of the oocyte.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4

claim: A robust reduction of the 1D5 signal was observed in TTLL5 mutant ovaries
source: We observed a robust reduction of the 1D5 signal in TTLL5 mutant ovaries, revealing that TTLL5 is essential for the appearance of polyglutamylated microtubules in the ovaries.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4

claim: TTLL5 is essential for the appearance of polyglutamylated microtubules in the ovaries
source: We observed a robust reduction of the 1D5 signal in TTLL5 mutant ovaries, revealing that TTLL5 is essential for the appearance of polyglutamylated microtubules in the ovaries.
evidence: Inference based on immunofluorescence data showing loss of 1D5 signal in TTLL5 mutants

claim: Staufen/osk mRNA localization requires the dynein/dynactin-mediated minus-end transport machinery in the early stages of oogenesis
source: Staufen/osk mRNA localization requires the dynein/dynactin-mediated minus-end transport machinery in the early stages of oogenesis.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: Staufen/osk mRNA becomes localized to the posterior of the oocyte from the mid to late stages of oogenesis, depending on kinesin-driven processes
source: Subsequently, the Staufen/osk mRNA becomes localized to the posterior of the oocyte from the mid to late stages of oogenesis. This localization phase depends on kinesin-driven processes, which include active transport and ooplasmic streaming in S10B oocytes (Kato and Nakamura, 2012; Lu et al., 2018; Brendza et al., 2000; Zimyanin et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kato and Nakamura, 2012; Lu et al., 2018; Brendza et al., 2000; Zimyanin et al., 2008

claim: In wild-type S10B oocytes, the localization of Staufen appeared very tight on the cortex with little lateral extension
source: In the wild type, the localization of Staufen appeared very tight on the cortex with little lateral extension in S10B (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A

claim: In ovaries lacking functional TTLL5, the Staufen localization appeared more diffuse in the S10B egg chambers of all TTLL5 null mutants
source: In ovaries lacking functional TTLL5, the Staufen localization appeared more diffuse in the S10B egg chambers of all TTLL5 null mutants (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B

claim: The broader expansion of the Staufen crescent was fully reversed in all UAS-Venus::TTLL5 rescued strains
source: The broader expansion of the Staufen crescent was fully reversed in all UAS-Venus::TTLL5 rescued strains (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C

claim: TTLL5 is required for tight cortical accumulation of Staufen in S10 oocytes
source: These results show that TTLL5 is required for tight cortical accumulation of Staufen in S10 oocytes.
evidence: Inference based on immunofluorescence data showing diffuse Staufen in TTLL5 mutants and rescue

claim: The requirement for TTLL5 for tight cortical accumulation of Staufen is a cell-autonomous one
source: Because the rescue construct was only expressed in the germline, they also strongly suggest that this requirement is a cell-autonomous one.
evidence: Inference based on germline-specific rescue of the Staufen phenotype

claim: Venus::TTLL5 strongly accumulated in the oocyte, especially along the cortex
source: Antibody staining suggested that Venus::TTLL5 strongly accumulated in the oocyte, especially along the cortex (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Venus::TTLL5 exhibited a cortical preference in S10B oocytes
source: Although the Venus fluorescence was relatively weak, Venus::TTLL5 exhibited a cortical preference in S10B oocytes, similar to that found by antibody staining (Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence data shown in Appendix 1—figure 3

claim: The stronger cortical accumulation of Venus::TTLL5 coincides with the region where polyglutamylated microtubules were enriched at S10B stage
source: This stronger cortical accumulation of Venus::TTLL5 coincides also with the region where polyglutamylated microtubules were enriched at the same stage (Figure 4).
evidence: Inference based on comparison of Venus::TTLL5 localization and 1D5 signal distribution

claim: In TTLL5 point mutants where the enzymatic activity was blocked, the localization pattern of Staufen was not refined and remained less tightly focused
source: In the TTLL5 point mutants, where specifically the enzymatic activity of TTLL5 was blocked (TTLL5E517A/-, TTLL5P522A/-, TTLL5R339A/-) the localization pattern of Staufen was not refined and the Staufen signal remained less tightly focused (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5D

claim: The length of the posterior Staufen crescent was significantly increased in TTLL5 null and TTLL5 point mutant ovaries compared to the control and UAS-Venus::TTLL5 rescued ovaries
source: Indeed, we found that the length of the posterior Staufen crescent was significantly increased in TTLL5 null and TTLL5 point mutant ovaries compared to the control and UAS-Venus::TTLL5 rescued ovaries (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5E

claim: No clear differences in Staufen distribution were observed between the wild type and TTLL5 mutants in S9 and earlier, previtellogenic stages of oogenesis
source: We did not observe clear differences in Staufen distribution between the wild type and TTLL5 mutants in S9 and earlier, previtellogenic stages of oogenesis (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5F

claim: The requirement for TTLL5 for tight cortical accumulation of Staufen starts around S10
source: Altogether, these results suggest that the requirement for TTLL5 for tight cortical accumulation of Staufen starts around S10 and the proper refinement of Staufen localization requires glutamylation of α-tubulin.
evidence: Inference based on stage-specific differences in Staufen localization phenotype

claim: The proper refinement of Staufen localization requires glutamylation of α-tubulin
source: Altogether, these results suggest that the requirement for TTLL5 for tight cortical accumulation of Staufen starts around S10 and the proper refinement of Staufen localization requires glutamylation of α-tubulin.
evidence: Inference based on phenotypes in enzymatic mutants of TTLL5

claim: Ooplasmic streaming contributes to the refinement of the posterior localization of Staufen
source: Ooplasmic streaming is a process that contributes to the refinement of the posterior localization of Staufen (Lu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lu et al., 2016

claim: Slow and nondirectional flows initiate at stages 8–9 and are followed by rapid and circular streaming at S10B
source: Slow and nondirectional flows initiate at stages 8–9 and are followed by rapid and circular streaming at S10B (Lu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lu et al., 2016

claim: All control ovaries had a typical streaming pattern with vesicles moving unidirectionally parallel to the cortex with a streaming center in the central part of the oocyte
source: All control ovaries had a typical streaming pattern, and the vesicles were moving unidirectionally parallel to the cortex with a streaming center in the central part of the oocyte.
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 6 and Videos 1-5

claim: 76% TTLL5MiEx/- and all TTLL5E517A/- mutant ovaries displayed abnormal streaming patterns
source: However, 76% TTLL5MiEx/- and all TTLL5E517A/- mutant ovaries displayed abnormal streaming patterns.
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 6 and Videos

claim: The typical streaming pattern was restored in 71% TTLL5MiEx/- ovaries expressing a Venus::TTLL5 rescue construct
source: The typical streaming pattern was restored in 71% TTLL5MiEx/- ovaries expressing a Venus::TTLL5 rescue construct.
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 6 and Videos

claim: 29% of the oocytes overexpressing Venus::TTLL5 displayed an abnormal streaming movement or a weak streaming flow
source: 29% of the oocytes displayed an abnormal streaming movement or a weak streaming flow like the one observed in TTLL5 mutants.
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 6 and Videos

claim: The onset of unidirectional fast streaming in S10B oocytes requires normal levels of TTLL5
source: We thus conclude that the onset of unidirectional fast streaming in S10B oocytes requires normal levels of TTLL5.
evidence: Inference based on streaming defects in both TTLL5 mutants and overexpression

claim: TTLL5 acts on the ooplasmic streaming through its role in MT glutamylation
source: Again, because abnormal streaming was observed when the enzymatic glutamylation activity of TTLL5 was impaired (TTLL5E517A/-), our results suggest that TTLL5 acts on the ooplasmic streaming through its role in MT glutamylation.
evidence: Inference based on streaming defects in enzymatic mutant

claim: The expression levels of ovarian Kinesin heavy chain (Khc) were neither affected by lack of TTLL5 function nor by TTLL5 overexpression
source: Firstly, the expression levels of ovarian Kinesin heavy chain (Khc) were neither affected by lack of TTLL5 function (Figure 7A) nor by TTLL5 overexpression (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7A and 7B

claim: Out of 37 wild-type oocytes, 76% showed a posteriorly enriched Khc signal in S10B
source: Out of 37 wild-type oocytes, 76% showed a posteriorly enriched Khc signal (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7D

claim: Khc distribution showed a posterior oocyte enrichment in only 13% and 14%, respectively, in TTLL5pBac/- and TTLL5MiEx/- mutant egg chambers
source: In contrast, Khc distribution showed a posterior oocyte enrichment in only 13% and 14%, respectively, in TTLL5pBac/- and TTLL5MiEx/- mutant egg chambers, respectively (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7C and D

claim: A smaller fraction of oocytes (54%) displayed clear posterior Khc enrichment upon elevated expression levels of TTLL5 than in the control
source: Elevated expression levels of TTLL5 seemed to affect Khc posterior accumulation as well because a smaller fraction of oocytes (54%) displayed clear posterior Khc enrichment than in the control (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7C and D

claim: Normal levels of TTLL5 are needed for the proper posterior enrichment of Khc in S10B oocytes
source: These results demonstrate that normal levels of TTLL5 are needed for the proper posterior enrichment of Khc in S10B oocytes.
evidence: Inference based on Khc localization defects in both TTLL5 mutants and overexpression

claim: Khc showed an additional higher accumulation in the inner part of the oocytes in 76% of wild-type oocytes
source: Khc showed an additional higher accumulation in the inner part of the oocytes (arrowhead in Figure 7E) and this was seen in 76% of the oocytes (Figure 7F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7E and F

claim: In the TTLL5 mutants, the inner accumulation of Khc was strongly reduced or absent
source: In the TTLL5 mutants, the inner accumulation of Khc was strongly reduced or absent (Figure 7E and G, Appendix 1—figure 4).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7E and G, Appendix 1—figure 4

claim: Only 19% of TTLL5pBac/- and 14% of TTLL5MiEx/- oocytes showed a slight inner Khc accumulation
source: Only 19% of TTLL5pBac/- and 14% of TTLL5MiEx/- oocytes showed a slight inner Khc accumulation (Figure 7F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7F

claim: Overexpressing TTLL5 in wild-type oocytes showed an inner peak of Khc accumulation in 65%
source: Overexpressing TTLL5 in wild-type oocytes showed an inner peak of Khc accumulation in 65%, which is slightly less than the wild-type control.
evidence: Supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data

claim: Higher levels of TTLL5 led to the appearance of two peaks of internal Khc accumulation in the oocyte, an anterior and a posterior one
source: Besides, the center of the single peak appeared in a more anterior position (Appendix 1—figure 4). Interestingly, the higher levels of TTLL5 also led to the appearance of two peaks of internal Khc accumulation in the oocyte, an anterior and a posterior one (Figure 7E and G and Appendix 1—figure 4).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7E and G and Appendix 1—figure 4

claim: Khc is causally connected to the fast cytoplasmic streaming
source: This suggests that Khc is causally connected to the fast cytoplasmic streaming, and both Khc localization and Khc-mediated streaming need TTLL5.
evidence: Inference based on correlation between Khc localization and streaming patterns

claim: Both Khc localization and Khc-mediated streaming need TTLL5
source: This suggests that Khc is causally connected to the fast cytoplasmic streaming, and both Khc localization and Khc-mediated streaming need TTLL5.
evidence: Inference based on phenotypes in TTLL5 mutants

claim: The expression levels of BicD were not affected by the TTLL5 levels
source: The expression levels of BicD were not affected by the TTLL5 levels (Appendix 1—figure 5).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Appendix 1—figure 5

claim: BicD localized to the posterior of the oocytes, and the ratio of the oocytes showing posteriorly localized BicD was similar in controls and TTLL5 mutants
source: Also, BicD localized to the posterior of the oocytes, and the ratio of the oocytes showing posteriorly localized BicD was similar in controls and TTLL5 mutants (Appendix 1—figure 5B and C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Appendix 1—figure 5B and C

claim: The dynein/dynactin/BicD transport on early oogenesis microtubules does not appear to depend on TTLL5
source: In conclusion and as suggested by the normal appearance of the egg chambers (see next paragraph), at least the dynein/dynactin/BicD transport on early oogenesis microtubules does not appear to depend on TTLL5.
evidence: Inference based on normal BicD localization in TTLL5 mutants

claim: The lack of TTLL5 neither caused a significant decrease in hatching rates, nor distinguishable morphological changes in ovaries
source: However, the lack of TTLL5 neither caused a significant decrease in hatching rates, nor distinguishable morphological changes in ovaries.
evidence: Supported by observations of egg chamber morphology and hatching rates

claim: The overall MT polarity of stage 10B oocytes was normal in TTLL5 mutants based on the localization of the polarity markers Gurken and Staufen protein
source: The overall MT polarity of stage 10B oocytes was normal in TTLL5 mutants based on the localization of the polarity markers Gurken and Staufen protein (Appendix 1—figure 6; Neuman-Silberberg and Schüpbach, 1996; Zimyanin et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Appendix 1—figure 6 and citations

claim: Mitochondria transported toward the thorax in wing nerves move by plus-end transport driven by kinesin
source: Specifically, we tracked the movement of GFP-labeled mitochondria (Mito::GFP) within the axon bundles of the arch in the L1 region (Vagnoni and Bullock, 2016; Figure 8A). The mitochondria transported toward the thorax move by plus-end transport, which is driven by kinesin, whereas mitochondria transported oppositely are transported by dynein (Vagnoni and Bullock, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vagnoni and Bullock, 2016

claim: Mitochondria transported away from the thorax in wing nerves are transported by dynein
source: The mitochondria transported toward the thorax move by plus-end transport, which is driven by kinesin, whereas mitochondria transported oppositely are transported by dynein (Vagnoni and Bullock, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vagnoni and Bullock, 2016

claim: For anterograde transport, the run length of mitochondria was similar between wild-type controls and TTLL5E517A/-
source: For the anterograde transport, the run length of mitochondria was similar between wild-type controls and TTLL5E517A/- (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative tracking data shown in Figure 8C

claim: A significant increase was observed in the total run velocity in TTLL5 E517A/- compared to wild-type controls for anterograde transport
source: However, a significant increase was observed in the total run velocity in TTLL5 E517A/- compared to wild-type controls (Figure 8D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative tracking data shown in Figure 8D

claim: The transport velocity of mitochondria was not affected by TTLL5E517A/- mutation for anterograde transport
source: Whereas the transport velocity of mitochondria was not affected (Figure 8E), the lack of the glutamylase activity had a striking effect on the pausing time of the anterograde transport of mitochondria, which was reduced by approximately 1.4 times (Figure 8F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative tracking data shown in Figure 8E

claim: The lack of the glutamylase activity reduced the pausing time of the anterograde transport of mitochondria by approximately 1.4 times
source: Whereas the transport velocity of mitochondria was not affected (Figure 8E), the lack of the glutamylase activity had a striking effect on the pausing time of the anterograde transport of mitochondria, which was reduced by approximately 1.4 times (Figure 8F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative tracking data shown in Figure 8F

claim: TTLL5 may not directly influence the transport process but instead modulate the pausing events during mitochondrial transport
source: This finding suggested that TTLL5 may not directly influence the transport process but instead modulate the pausing events during mitochondrial transport.
evidence: Inference based on unchanged transport velocity but reduced pausing time

claim: A higher frequency of pausing was observed in the control group compared to the TTLL5E517A/- mutant for anterograde transport
source: Notably, a higher frequency of pausing was observed in the control group compared to the TTLL5E517A/- mutant.
evidence: Supported by kymograph analysis shown in Figure 8G

claim: The control exhibited a 1.5 times greater frequency of pausing compared to the TTLL5E517A/- mutant for anterograde transport
source: By analyzing the pausing events within a given distance, we found that the control exhibited a 1.5 times greater frequency of pausing compared to the TTLL5E517A/- mutant (Figure 8H).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 8H

claim: The longer total pausing time in controls can be attributed to a higher frequency of pausing events during anterograde transport
source: These results indicate that the longer total pausing time in controls can be attributed to a higher frequency of pausing events during anterograde transport.
evidence: Inference based on pausing frequency analysis

claim: No significant changes were observed in the parameters of retrograde transport in TTLL5 mutants
source: In contrast, we did not observe significant changes in the parameters of retrograde transport in TTLL5 mutants, indicating that dynein-based transport was not affected.
evidence: Supported by quantitative tracking data shown in Figure 8

claim: Dynein-based transport was not affected by TTLL5 mutation
source: In contrast, we did not observe significant changes in the parameters of retrograde transport in TTLL5 mutants, indicating that dynein-based transport was not affected.
evidence: Inference based on unchanged retrograde transport parameters

claim: The glutamylation activity of TTLL5 plays a role in regulating the pausing of anterograde axonal transport
source: To sum up, these results show that the glutamylation activity of TTLL5 plays a role in regulating the pausing of anterograde axonal transport.
evidence: Inference based on effects of enzymatic mutant on mitochondrial pausing

claim: TTLL5 is essential for the normal glutamylation of the ovarian αTub84B/D
source: Our results revealed that TTLL5 is essential for the normal glutamylation of the ovarian αTub84B/D.
evidence: Supported by MS and western blot data showing loss of glutamylation in TTLL5 mutants

claim: Even in wild-type ovaries, the oogenesis-specific aTub67C was not glutamylated
source: Surprisingly, even in wild-type ovaries, the oogenesis-specific aTub67C was not glutamylated, suggesting that this gene, αTub67C, may have evolved to produce MTs that contain regions that are less glutamylated.
evidence: Supported by MS data showing no glutamylation on αTub67C

claim: αTub67C may have evolved to produce MTs that contain regions that are less glutamylated
source: Surprisingly, even in wild-type ovaries, the oogenesis-specific aTub67C was not glutamylated, suggesting that this gene, αTub67C, may have evolved to produce MTs that contain regions that are less glutamylated.
evidence: Speculation based on the observation that αTub67C is not glutamylated

claim: TTLL5 is required for the proper distribution of Kinesin heavy chain (Khc)
source: We found that TTLL5 is required for the proper distribution of Kinesin heavy chain (Khc), for proper cytoplasmic streaming during late oogenesis, as well as for fine-tuning the localization of the Staufen protein.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing altered Khc distribution in TTLL5 mutants

claim: TTLL5 is required for proper cytoplasmic streaming during late oogenesis
source: We found that TTLL5 is required for the proper distribution of Kinesin heavy chain (Khc), for proper cytoplasmic streaming during late oogenesis, as well as for fine-tuning the localization of the Staufen protein.
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data showing streaming defects in TTLL5 mutants

claim: TTLL5 is required for fine-tuning the localization of the Staufen protein
source: We found that TTLL5 is required for the proper distribution of Kinesin heavy chain (Khc), for proper cytoplasmic streaming during late oogenesis, as well as for fine-tuning the localization of the Staufen protein.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing diffuse Staufen localization in TTLL5 mutants

claim: TTLL5 promotes the pausing of mitochondria during anterograde axonal transport in wing nerves
source: Furthermore, TTLL5 promotes the pausing of mitochondria during anterograde axonal transport in wing nerves.
evidence: Supported by mitochondrial tracking data showing reduced pausing in TTLL5 mutants

claim: Mammalian TTLL5 is considered to be an initiator glutamylase
source: TTLL5 has the enzymatic activity to add glutamyl groups and mammalian TTLL5 is considered to be an initiator glutamylase (van Dijk et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to van Dijk et al., 2007

claim: TTLL1 and TTLL6 are elongators of polyglutamylation of α-tubulin
source: TTLL1 and TTLL6 are elongators of polyglutamylation of α-tubulin (Gadadhar et al., 2017; van Dijk et al., 2007; Janke et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gadadhar et al., 2017; van Dijk et al., 2007; Janke et al., 2005

claim: There is no evidence that the homologous TTLL6A/TTLL6B or TTLL1A/1B are expressed in Drosophila ovaries
source: However, there is no evidence that the homologous TTLL6A/TTLL6B or TTLL1A/1B are expressed in Drosophila ovaries (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by expression data in Supplementary file 1

claim: TTLL5 is needed, directly or indirectly, for polyglutamylation in Drosophila
source: The robust reduction of polyglutamylated tubulin in TTLL5 mutants observed in ovaries (this work) and the nervous system (Devambez et al., 2017) further shows that TTLL5 is also needed, directly or indirectly, for polyglutamylation in Drosophila.
evidence: Inference based on loss of polyglutamylation signal in TTLL5 mutants

claim: The unidirectional flow seen during rapid ooplasmic streaming is caused by the kinesin-1-dependent MT sliding and MT cargo transport along the cortical and subcortical MTs
source: The unidirectional flow seen during rapid ooplasmic streaming is caused by the kinesin-1-dependent MT sliding and MT cargo transport along the cortical and subcortical MTs (Lu et al., 2016; Monteith et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lu et al., 2016 and Monteith et al., 2016

claim: The proper localization of Khc to the posterior cortical region depends on TTLL5
source: The proper localization of Khc to the posterior cortical region (Figure 7) and the glutamylation of cortical MTs (Figure 4) depend on TTLL5, which is normally also concentrated at the cortex in S10B oocytes (Figure 5C and Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: Inference based on altered Khc localization in TTLL5 mutants shown in Figure 7

claim: The glutamylation of cortical MTs depends on TTLL5
source: The proper localization of Khc to the posterior cortical region (Figure 7) and the glutamylation of cortical MTs (Figure 4) depend on TTLL5, which is normally also concentrated at the cortex in S10B oocytes (Figure 5C and Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: Supported by loss of 1D5 signal in TTLL5 mutants shown in Figure 4

claim: Glutamylation of the MTs is a precondition for the proper function of kinesin-1
source: All these observations point to the role of glutamylation of the MTs as a precondition for the proper function of kinesin-1.
evidence: Inference based on multiple observations linking TTLL5, glutamylation, and kinesin-1 function

claim: The inner-oocyte MTs might contribute to the rapid streaming observed
source: Kinesin-1 also accumulates at higher levels in the inner part of the oocyte (Figure 7), suggesting that the inner-oocyte MTs might also contribute to the rapid streaming observed.
evidence: Speculation based on inner Khc accumulation shown in Figure 7

claim: α-tubulin was the only tubulin subunit that can be glutamylated in the Drosophila nervous system
source: The previous study showed that α-tubulin was the only tubulin subunit that can be glutamylated in the Drosophila nervous system and TTLL5 is required for α-tubulin glutamylation in the neurons (Devambez et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Devambez et al., 2017

claim: The absence of TTLL5 did not reveal clear defects in larval neuromuscular junction morphology, larval locomotion behavior, or vesicular axonal transport in larval neurons
source: However, the absence of TTLL5 did not reveal clear defects in larval neuromuscular junction morphology, larval locomotion behavior, or vesicular axonal transport in larval neurons.
evidence: Stated as a summary of previous findings

claim: Glutamylated α-tubulins promoted the normal stopping or pausing of mitochondria during axonal transport
source: By measuring the parameters related to the pausing time and pause frequency, we found that glutamylated α-tubulins promoted the normal stopping or pausing of mitochondria during axonal transport.
evidence: Inference based on reduced pausing in TTLL5 mutants

claim: Glutamylated sidechains of α-tubulin might act as marks or even obstacles that disturb the movement of mitochondria
source: Glutamylated sidechains of α-tubulin might act as marks or even obstacles that disturb the movement of mitochondria.
evidence: Speculation based on the observed effects on mitochondrial pausing

claim: The absence of polyglutamylation of α-tubulin in TTLL1-/- increased the motility of mitochondria in the mouse neurons but did not affect their transport velocity
source: Moreover, a previous study revealed a similar function of glutamylation of α-tubulin for the transport of mitochondria (Bodakuntla et al., 2021). The absence of polyglutamylation of α-tubulin in TTLL1-/- increased the motility of mitochondria in the mouse neurons but did not affect their transport velocity.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bodakuntla et al., 2021

claim: Glutamylation of α-tubulin may not directly affect transport but rather affect mitochondrial docking and motor binding to MT tracks by acting as roadblocks on the MT tracks
source: The results led to their hypothesis that glutamylation of α-tubulin may not directly affect transport but rather affect mitochondrial docking and motor binding to MT tracks by acting as roadblocks on the MT tracks.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from another study cited in the discussion

claim: Glutamylation of MTs plays a role in controlling kinesin-1 activity
source: Our results showed a selective effect of Glu-MTs on mitochondrial motility for plus-end transport in axons, a process that is carried out by kinesin-1 (Pilling et al., 2006). This suggests that glutamylation of MTs plays a role in controlling kinesin-1 activity similar to what we had observed in the stage 10B oocyte.
evidence: Inference based on selective effects on anterograde transport and citation to Pilling et al., 2006

claim: The considerable negative charge of the modified regions in the poly-Glu-modified tubulins might interfere with the interaction of kinesin with tubulin
source: The considerable negative charge of the modified regions in the poly-Glu-modified tubulins might interfere with the interaction of kinesin with tubulin (Figure 1B; Skiniotis et al., 2004).
evidence: Speculation supported by citation to Skiniotis et al., 2004

claim: TTLL7-modified β-tubulin polyglutamylation specifically decreases the motility of kinesin-1 in vitro
source: More recent in vitro studies further reveal that TTLL7-modified β-tubulin polyglutamylation specifically decreases the motility of kinesin-1 (Genova et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Genova et al., 2023

claim: Sidechain glutamylation of MTs is sensed by kinesin-1 and functions to interfere with the MT binding of kinesin-1
source: All these observations suggest that sidechain glutamylation of MTs is sensed by kinesin-1 and functions to interfere with the MT binding of kinesin-1, thus disturbing the movement of kinesin-1-dependent cargos.
evidence: Inference based on multiple lines of evidence from this study and others

claim: An essential function of α-tubulin glutamylation has not emerged from this study
source: Even though an essential function of α-tubulin glutamylation has not emerged from this study, it has become clear that kinesin-1-dependent processes are modified or controlled by this modification and that evolution has adapted the tubulin code to optimize the usage of MTs for different evolving needs.
evidence: Inference based on the overall findings showing modulation but not essentiality

claim: Kinesin-1-dependent processes are modified or controlled by α-tubulin glutamylation
source: Even though an essential function of α-tubulin glutamylation has not emerged from this study, it has become clear that kinesin-1-dependent processes are modified or controlled by this modification and that evolution has adapted the tubulin code to optimize the usage of MTs for different evolving needs.
evidence: Inference based on multiple observations of kinesin-1-dependent phenotypes in TTLL5 mutants

claim: Evolution has adapted the tubulin code to optimize the usage of MTs for different evolving needs
source: Even though an essential function of α-tubulin glutamylation has not emerged from this study, it has become clear that kinesin-1-dependent processes are modified or controlled by this modification and that evolution has adapted the tubulin code to optimize the usage of MTs for different evolving needs.
evidence: Speculation based on the differential glutamylation of different α-tubulin isotypes

claim: TTLL5 is not essential for survival
source: That TTLL5 is not essential for survival also makes this protein an interesting candidate drug target to modulate its glutamylation activity to regulate and possibly even increase MT transport in neurodegenerative diseases where MT transport is known to be affected (Bodakuntla et al., 2020).
evidence: Inference based on viability of TTLL5 mutants

claim: TTLL5 is an interesting candidate drug target to modulate its glutamylation activity to regulate and possibly even increase MT transport in neurodegenerative diseases
source: That TTLL5 is not essential for survival also makes this protein an interesting candidate drug target to modulate its glutamylation activity to regulate and possibly even increase MT transport in neurodegenerative diseases where MT transport is known to be affected (Bodakuntla et al., 2020).
evidence: Speculation based on findings and citation to Bodakuntla et al., 2020
